terms.name: Database
terms.definition: An organised collection of data that can be accessed by different application programs.
terms.example: The school attendance and reporting applications use the same student database.

terms.name: Relational database
terms.definition: A database that represents data in related tables; matching key values implement links between them.
terms.example: Student.ClassID links a student to a row in Class.

terms.name: Table
terms.definition: A collection of rows about one kind of entity, organised into named columns.
terms.example: Student stores one row per student.

terms.name: Record
terms.definition: A row in a database table.
terms.example: The complete row for Noor is one record.

terms.name: Field
terms.definition: A column in a database table.
terms.example: DateOfBirth is a field in Student.

terms.name: Tuple
terms.definition: One instance of an entity represented by a row in a relational table.
terms.example: The S1276 row is a tuple; it is also a record.

terms.name: Entity
terms.definition: Something about which data is stored, such as a person, place, object or event.
terms.example: Student, Class and Teacher are entity types in our school model.

terms.name: Attribute
terms.definition: A named data item stored about an entity.
terms.example: A student has the attributes StudentID and FirstName.

terms.name: Candidate key
terms.definition: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row. No smaller subset does the same job.
terms.example: If both StudentID and SchoolEmail are guaranteed unique, each can be a candidate key.

terms.name: Primary key
terms.definition: The candidate key selected to identify each row uniquely.
terms.example: StudentID identifies the student, even when two students share a name.

terms.name: Secondary key
terms.definition: In this Hodder chapter, a candidate key that is an alternative to the selected primary key.
terms.example: SchoolEmail is a secondary key when StudentID is selected as the primary key.

terms.name: Foreign key
terms.definition: Attribute(s) whose values refer to a key in another table; this chapter uses references to primary keys.
terms.example: Student.ClassID references Class.ClassID.

terms.name: Relationship
terms.definition: A link between entities, implemented in this chapter by a foreign key referencing a primary key.
terms.example: Many Student rows are linked to one Class row.

terms.name: Referential integrity
terms.definition: Every non-null foreign-key value must match a referenced key value.
terms.example: A student cannot use ClassID 9Z when Class contains only 7A and 7B.

terms.name: Index
terms.definition: An additional data structure built from one or more columns to make searching faster.
terms.example: An index on ClassID, SecondName and FirstName helps find an alphabetical class list.

terms.name: Entity-relationship (E-R) model or E-R diagram
terms.definition: A visual model showing entities and the relationships between them.
terms.example: The school diagram links Class to Student and Student to Subject through StudentSubject.

terms.name: Normalisation
terms.definition: Organising tables and relationships to reduce unnecessary repetition and undesirable dependencies.
terms.example: Keep the class location in Class instead of copying it into every student row.

terms.name: First normal form (1NF)
terms.definition: A table has no repeating groups; each attribute value holds one value from its domain.
terms.example: Store each student–subject choice in a separate StudentSubject row.

terms.name: Second normal form (2NF)
terms.definition: A table is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not just part of it.
terms.example: SubjectTeacher depends on SubjectName alone, so it leaves the table keyed by (StudentID, SubjectName).

terms.name: Third normal form (3NF)
terms.definition: At this level: a table is in 2NF and has no dependencies between non-key attributes.
terms.example: ClassID determines Location; keep Location in Class rather than Student.

terms.name: Composite key
terms.definition: A key made from two or more attributes used together to identify a row.
terms.example: (StudentID, SubjectName) identifies one subject choice per student.

terms.name: Database management system (DBMS)
terms.definition: System software used to define, create, manage and manipulate a database.
terms.example: A DBMS checks keys and permissions when the school updates a student.

terms.name: Data management
terms.definition: Organising and maintaining stored data so that the required information can be produced.
terms.example: Entering students, correcting addresses and retrieving class lists.

terms.name: Data dictionary
terms.definition: A collection of metadata describing the database.
terms.example: It records the StudentID data type, key constraint and table membership.

terms.name: Data modelling
terms.definition: Analysing the data requirements and defining the structures and relationships needed.
terms.example: Identify Student and Class, then specify their attributes and relationship.

terms.name: Logical schema
terms.definition: A model of a particular database independent of the DBMS implementation.
terms.example: STUDENT(StudentID, FirstName, ClassID) and its relationship to CLASS.

terms.name: Access rights
terms.definition: Permissions controlling which data a user can access and which actions they can perform.
terms.example: A pupil reads their own timetable; an administrator can update class assignments.

terms.name: Developer interface
terms.definition: The DBMS facilities through which a developer defines and manipulates a database.
terms.example: A developer writes CREATE TABLE and SELECT commands in an SQL interface.

terms.name: Structured query language (SQL)
terms.definition: A standard language used to define relational structures and retrieve or modify their data.
terms.example: CREATE TABLE defines a table; SELECT retrieves rows.

terms.name: Query processor
terms.definition: The DBMS component that processes and executes queries.
terms.example: It interprets DDL or compiles and optimises DML before evaluation.

terms.name: Data definition language (DDL)
terms.definition: Commands used to create, change or remove database structures.
terms.example: CREATE TABLE Student defines columns and keys.

terms.name: Data manipulation language (DML)
terms.definition: Commands used to retrieve, add, change or remove stored data.
terms.example: SELECT retrieves rows; UPDATE changes their values.

terms.name: SQL script
terms.definition: A sequence of SQL commands for a task, often saved for reuse.
terms.example: A school setup script creates tables and inserts initial rows.

lessons.title: Read one simple table
lessons.subtitle: Rows, columns and values — before database design.
objectives: Identify entity, table, record, field, tuple and attribute.
Distinguish an attribute name from a value.
Describe one entity instance using its row.
lessons.hook: Is “Noor” an attribute, a record, or the value of an attribute?

blocks.title: Start with three students
blocks.text: The school needs to remember each student’s name and class. This table organises those facts into rows and columns.
blocks.uz: Maktab har bir o‘quvchining ismi va sinfini saqlamoqchi. Jadvalga qarang: Noor 7A da, Ahmad 7B da, Tahir 7A da o‘qiydi. Hozircha faqat jadvalni o‘qishni o‘rganamiz.

blocks.title: One row tells us about one student
blocks.text: Read across: S1276, Noor, 7A. Together these values describe one student. The whole row is a record. In a relational table, another name for a row is tuple.
blocks.uz: Bitta katak emas, Noor haqidagi butun qator record deyiladi. Relational database da shu qatorning yana bir nomi — tuple.
blocks.remember: Record = row. Tuple is another name for that row.

blocks.title: One column stores one kind of fact
blocks.text: Read down: every value is a first name. FirstName is a field (column). Its name tells us what kind of fact belongs here. Noor is one value in that field.
blocks.uz: FirstName ustunida faqat ismlar turibdi. Field — ustun, Noor esa shu ustundagi bitta qiymat. Ustun nomi bilan katakdagi qiymatni aralashtirmang.

blocks.title: Now name the thing and its properties
blocks.text: An entity is a thing we store data about, such as a student. An attribute is a property of that thing, such as FirstName. Student names the entity type; Noor is one particular student. The table stores many students of that type.
blocks.uz: Nima haqida ma’lumot saqlayapmiz? O‘quvchi haqida — bu entity. Uning qaysi xususiyatini saqlayapmiz? Ismini — bu attribute. Jadvalda attribute ustun orqali ifodalanadi.
blocks.remember: Student → entity. FirstName → attribute. Noor → value.

blocks.title: Point to a row, a column and a value
blocks.text: Use the buttons below. Each highlight shows a different part of the same table. Say what the highlighted part tells you before moving on.
blocks.uz: Tugmalarni bosib qator, ustun va katakni solishtiring. Har safar “bu bitta o‘quvchimi, bitta xususiyatmi yoki bitta qiymatmi?” deb o‘zingizga savol bering.

worked.prompt: In (S1277, Ahmad, 7B), what is the record and what is the FirstName value?
worked.answer: The record is the whole row: (S1277, Ahmad, 7B). FirstName is the column name. Ahmad is the value in that column.

checks.prompt: Which is the name of a column?
checks.why: FirstName labels a field. Noor is a value; the whole row is a record.

checks.prompt: Which gives all the stored facts about one student?
checks.why: A record is one complete row. Tuple is another name for that row.

recap: Record = row. Tuple is another name for that row.
Field = column. Noor = a value.
Student → entity. FirstName → attribute. Noor → value.
lessons.mistake: Do not describe a single cell as a record or confuse an attribute with its value.
lessons.next: Next: Why repeated files cause problems.

Look at one part at a time

items.title: Table
items.text: Student is the name of this whole collection of student rows.

items.title: Record / tuple
items.text: S1276 | Noor | Baig | 7A is one complete row about one student.

items.title: Field / attribute
items.text: FirstName is a column; its name tells us what kind of data is stored there.

items.title: Value
items.text: Noor is one value in the FirstName column, not the name of a field.

details.title: Entity: what are we describing?
details.text: An entity is something we store information about, for example a student or a class. Student describes the entity type. An individual student is one instance, represented by a row (tuple). An attribute is one named fact about that entity, such as FirstName.
details.uz: Student — kim haqidagi ma’lumot saqlanayotganini bildiradi. FirstName — attribute; Noor — shu attribute qiymati.

details.title: Six terms on one screen
rows: FirstName: a named property of Student

worked.prompt: For the S1277 row, identify the entity type, one attribute, its value, and the tuple.
worked.answer: Entity type: Student. Attribute: FirstName. Value: Ahmad. Tuple: (S1277, Ahmad, Sayed, 7B).
criteria: Include every value when identifying the tuple.

checks.prompt: What does the complete row for S1299 represent?
checks.why: A row stores one instance of an entity.

checks.prompt: A school wants to store teachers. Name the entity and two possible attributes.
checks.answer: Teacher is an entity. Possible attributes include LicenceNumber and TeacherName.

lessons.title: Why repeated files cause problems
lessons.subtitle: Follow one address change in two offices.
objectives: Describe records and fields in a file.
Distinguish redundancy, inconsistency and data dependency.
Explain a concrete consequence of each limitation.
lessons.hook: Payroll changes a teacher’s staff number. Sales still uses the old number. Which record is now correct?

blocks.title: Two offices keep Noor’s address
blocks.text: Both offices store the same address. Keeping unnecessary copies of the same fact is data redundancy.
blocks.uz: Bitta manzil ikki faylda saqlangan. Shu bir xil ma’lumotni ortiqcha takrorlab saqlash data redundancy deyiladi. Hali ikkala nusxa ham to‘g‘ri.

blocks.title: Noor moves. Only one copy is updated.
blocks.text: Now the copies disagree. This is data inconsistency. The library may send a letter to the old address because its copy was missed.
blocks.uz: Noor ko‘chdi. Maktab manzilni yangiladi, kutubxona esa yangilamadi. Endi nusxalar bir-biriga mos emas: bu data inconsistency. Sababi — bir o‘zgarishni ikki joyga kiritish kerak edi.
blocks.remember: Redundancy: repeated facts. Inconsistency: conflicting facts.

blocks.title: A program expects a fixed field order
blocks.text: The old program reads field 2 as the address. After Phone is inserted, field 2 contains a phone number. The program must change because it depends on the file layout. This is data dependency.
blocks.uz: Dastur “2-o‘rinda manzil turadi” deb ishlaydi. Oldiga Phone qo‘shilsa, manzil 3-o‘ringa o‘tadi. Dastur eski tartibga bog‘liq bo‘lgani uchun uni ham o‘zgartirish kerak. Bu — data dependency.

blocks.title: Three problems, three different questions
blocks.text: Is the same fact stored unnecessarily more than once? Redundancy. Do its copies disagree? Inconsistency. Must a program change when the file layout changes? Dependency. The next lesson shows how a database helps.
blocks.uz: Takror saqlanganmi — redundancy. Nusxalar farqlanib qolganmi — inconsistency. Fayl tuzilishi o‘zgarsa dastur ham o‘zgaradimi — dependency. Uchalasini bitta muammo deb yodlamang.

worked.prompt: The office has Noor’s new address, but the library has the old address. What went wrong?
worked.answer: The copies disagree: data inconsistency. Keeping two copies created the risk: data redundancy. Updating only one copy caused the disagreement.

checks.prompt: Two address copies now disagree. What is this?
checks.why: Inconsistency means the values disagree. Redundancy means storing unnecessary copies.

checks.prompt: A file’s field order changes and the program must change. What is this?
checks.why: The program depends on the file layout.

recap: Redundancy: repeated facts. Inconsistency: conflicting facts.
lessons.mistake: Repeated data is redundancy even before any copy becomes incorrect. Inconsistency occurs when copies disagree.

details.title: Two files about the same student
First, notice the duplicate
details.text: Both files describe the same student. StudentID, name and ClassID were copied. The ClassID values now disagree. A record is one student's complete row; a field stores one kind of fact, such as ClassID.
details.uz: Bir o‘quvchi haqidagi ma’lumot ikki joyga yozilgan. ClassID qiymatlari turlicha bo‘lib qolgan.

details.title: Three names for three different problems
rows: The same student facts are stored in both files.
One file says 7A and another says 7B.
A program expects fields in a particular order or structure; changing it may require changing the program.

details.title: What happened? Read the cause, then the effect

items.title: Copy
items.text: The school stores Noor's details in two separate files.

items.title: Change
items.text: A staff member changes ClassID in Attendance only.

items.title: Result
items.text: Exam still shows the old class. This is inconsistency caused by duplicated data.

details.title: A program expects a particular structure
details.text: A file is a collection of data. It may contain records, each made of fields about one thing. Records can have fixed or variable length; some carry structural information such as field count or record length. A program must know how to read that structure. If it changes, another program using it may need rewriting.
details.uz: File ichidagi field tartibi yoki uzunligi o‘zgarsa, eski tartibni kutayotgan dastur ma’lumotni noto‘g‘ri o‘qishi mumkin.

worked.prompt: Activity 8A adaptation: Payroll stores staff number 84 after an update; Sales still stores 42. Name the immediate problem and the underlying duplication problem.
worked.answer: The two files now disagree: data inconsistency. Storing the staff number twice is data redundancy. A changed field position would instead illustrate data dependency.

checks.prompt: The two files still have identical copies of Noor's address. What problem already exists?
checks.why: Unnecessary copies are redundancy even before they disagree.

checks.prompt: The Exam program stops reading correctly after a new column is inserted into its file. Name the limitation and explain why it happened.
checks.answer: Data dependency. The program expects a particular record structure, so inserting a column can cause it to read the wrong field.
criteria: Connect the error to the changed file structure.

lessons.title: Connect two small tables
lessons.subtitle: Find a student’s room without copying class details.
objectives: Define database and relational database.
Match the database approach to the three file-based limitations.
Explain data independence without claiming that every change is harmless.
lessons.hook: What if Payroll and Sales read the same staff record?

blocks.title: Keep one controlled student record
blocks.text: Instead of each office keeping its own address file, both applications can read the same student record. Update Noor’s address once; both see the new value. A database is an organised collection of data that applications can access.
blocks.uz: Maktab va kutubxona alohida manzil nusxalarini saqlash o‘rniga bitta boshqariladigan yozuvdan foydalanadi. Manzil bir marta yangilanadi. Database — tartiblangan, dasturlar foydalanishi mumkin bo‘lgan ma’lumotlar to‘plami.

blocks.title: Students still need their own table
blocks.text: The Student table answers: who is the student, and which class are they in? It does not need to store the classroom address in every row.
blocks.uz: Bu jadval o‘quvchining kimligini va qaysi sinfga tegishliligini saqlaydi. Sinfxona joylashuvini har bir o‘quvchi qatoriga qayta yozish shart emas.

blocks.title: Class facts belong in a Class table
blocks.text: To find Noor’s room, read 7A from Noor’s row, then find 7A here. The answer is Room 12. ClassID connects the two tables. A relational database stores related data in tables linked by key values.
blocks.uz: Noorning qatoridan 7A ni oldik. Class jadvalidan 7A ni topdik: xona — Room 12. Shu mos qiymat orqali jadvallar bog‘landi. Bunday jadvallardan tuzilgan baza relational database deyiladi.

blocks.title: What if 7A moves to Room 20?
blocks.text: Change Location once in the Class table. Noor and Tahir still have ClassID 7A, so both now link to Room 20. Repeating 7A in Student is useful: it records class membership. Repeating every class detail would be unnecessary.
blocks.uz: Faqat Class jadvalidagi 7A xonasini Room 20 ga almashtiramiz. Noor va Tahirning sinfi 7A bo‘lib qoladi. 7A takrorlanishi kerak: u o‘quvchining sinfini bildiradi. Xonaning manzilini qayta-qayta saqlash esa kerak emas.

blocks.title: The programs no longer read raw field positions
blocks.text: Database management software handles storage and access. Applications request named data instead of managing their own file layouts. This reduces data dependency. A program that needs a deleted field may still need changing.
blocks.uz: Ma’lumotni saqlash va olish ishini maxsus boshqaruv dasturi bajaradi. Ilova o‘z faylidagi ustun o‘rniga qattiq bog‘lanmaydi. Lekin ilovaga kerak bo‘lgan ustun o‘chirib yuborilsa, ilovani tuzatish baribir zarur bo‘lishi mumkin.

worked.prompt: Tahir belongs to 7A. Class 7A now has Location = Room 20. Where does Tahir go?
worked.answer: Read Tahir’s ClassID: 7A. Find 7A in Class. Read its Location: Room 20. No change to Tahir’s own row was needed.

checks.prompt: 7A moves room. Which value should change?
options: Location in the Class row for 7A
checks.why: Location is stored once with the class. Student rows keep their class link.

checks.prompt: Why is 7A allowed to repeat in Student?
options: It records that several students belong to 7A
Every value in a database must repeat
checks.why: Repeated ClassID values express membership without repeating all class details.

recap: Noor → 7A → Room 12.
lessons.mistake: “All data is stored exactly once” is too absolute. Foreign-key values repeat legitimately.
lessons.next: Next: Identify a row, then link it.

details.title: One source, two applications
Now the meaning
details.text: A database is an organised collection of data that different applications can access. Attendance and Exams can read the same Student row. A relational database uses related tables to organise facts; the connections between tables will be explained later.
details.uz: Endi ikkita dastur ma’lumotni alohida nusxalardan emas, bitta umumiy bazadan oladi.

details.title: Change one fact

items.title: Before
items.text: Noor belongs to 7A in the shared Student table.

items.title: Update
items.text: An authorised user changes that one ClassID value to 7B.

items.title: After
items.text: Attendance and Exams both read the new value from the same row.

details.title: Old problem → database benefit
rows: Avoid keeping a separate copy of each student in every application.
Controlled changes become available to all authorised applications.
The DBMS provides structured access instead of each program owning its own file layout.

details.title: One sensible limit
details.text: Data independence does not mean every possible database change is harmless. A program that still needs a deleted column may need changing. The database approach reduces this dependency.

worked.prompt: Amina’s address changes. Describe the update in the shared database approach.
worked.answer: Update the one staff record. Both authorised applications retrieve the same new address, reducing the risk of conflicting copies.

checks.prompt: Which setup best avoids two conflicting ClassID values?
options: One shared Student table read by both apps
Two separate copies that staff must update manually
checks.why: One controlled source reduces the risk of conflicting updates.

checks.prompt: Give one reason why the database approach is better than separate student files.
checks.answer: The same student details need not be stored separately for every application, reducing redundant data and the risk of inconsistent updates.
criteria: Explain the consequence for the school.

lessons.title: Identify a row, then link it
lessons.subtitle: Primary keys first; foreign and composite keys next.
objectives: Distinguish all five key types used in this chapter.
Check referential integrity.
Explain what an index does.
lessons.hook: Two students can share a name. What should identify each student?

blocks.title: Two students can have the same name
blocks.text: “Find Noor” is ambiguous. “Find S1276” identifies exactly one row. We choose StudentID as the primary key: the identifier for each row. It must be unique and cannot be missing.
blocks.uz: “Noorni top” desak, ikki qator chiqadi. “S1276 ni top” desak, bittasi chiqadi. Qatorni aniq ajratish uchun tanlangan kalit primary key deyiladi. U takrorlanmaydi va bo‘sh bo‘lmaydi.

blocks.title: Choose from the possible identifiers
blocks.text: Suppose the school guarantees that StudentID and SchoolEmail are each unique. Either could identify a student: each is a candidate key. Choose StudentID as the primary key. Hodder calls the unused candidate SchoolEmail a secondary key. A candidate key uses only the attributes needed for uniqueness.
blocks.uz: Maktab StudentID ham, SchoolEmail ham takrorlanmasligini kafolatlasa, ikkalasi candidate key bo‘la oladi. Ulardan StudentID ni asosiy kalit qilib tanlaymiz. Hodderdagi atama bo‘yicha qolgan SchoolEmail — secondary key. Ismlar bir namunada farqli ko‘ringani ularni kalit qilmaydi.

blocks.title: A foreign key points to a related row
blocks.text: Student.ClassID means the ClassID column in Student. It points to Class.ClassID, the primary key in Class. This makes Student.ClassID a foreign key. The link records a relationship: a student belongs to a class. Many students may have the same ClassID.
blocks.uz: Student.ClassID — Student jadvalidagi ClassID ustuni degani. U Class jadvalidagi 7A kabi kalitga murojaat qiladi: shuning uchun foreign key. Class jadvalida 7A bir marta, Student jadvalida esa ko‘p marta kelishi mumkin.
blocks.remember: Primary key identifies this row. Foreign key links to another table.

blocks.title: Can a student join class 9Z?
blocks.text: Only 7A and 7B exist below. Try choosing 9Z. A supplied foreign-key value must match an existing referenced key. This rule is referential integrity: a link must not point to a missing class.
blocks.uz: Quyida faqat 7A va 7B mavjud. 9Z ni tanlab ko‘ring: topilmaydi. Foreign key mavjud yozuvga bog‘lanishi shart. Referential integrity shu moslikni saqlaydi.

blocks.title: Sometimes one identifier needs two columns
blocks.text: S1276 appears twice. Maths appears twice. But each student–subject pair is different. If a student takes each subject once, (StudentID, SubjectName) identifies a row. This is a composite key: one key made from more than one attribute.
blocks.uz: StudentID yolg‘iz yetmaydi: S1276 ikki marta bor. SubjectName yolg‘iz yetmaydi: Maths ikki marta bor. Ikkalasini birga olsak, aniq tanlovni topamiz. Bu — composite key.

blocks.title: An index helps us find rows faster
blocks.text: A book index helps you find a topic without reading every page. A database index is an extra lookup structure that can help locate rows, for example by ClassID. It can contain repeated values. It speeds some searches but needs storage and updates when data changes.
blocks.uz: Kitob oxiridagi ko‘rsatkich mavzuni tez topishga yordam beradi. Database index ham qatorni topish uchun yordamchi tuzilma. Index — qatorning primary key ekanini yoki boshqa jadval bilan bog‘langanini o‘z-o‘zidan bildirmaydi.

worked.prompt: Which key identifies Noor’s student row, and which key tells us Noor’s class?
worked.answer: StudentID identifies the row: it is Student’s primary key. ClassID links that row to Class: it is a foreign key in Student.

checks.prompt: Class contains 7A and 7B. Which new Student.ClassID violates referential integrity?
checks.why: 9Z has no matching parent key in Class.

checks.prompt: In StudentSubject, why use (StudentID, SubjectName) as the key?
options: Both columns must separately be unique
Either column alone always identifies the row
Each column can repeat, but the pair identifies one choice
checks.why: S1276 can take several subjects and Maths can have several students. The pair identifies one choice.

recap: Primary key: which exact row?
Primary key identifies this row. Foreign key links to another table.
lessons.mistake: A foreign key is not automatically unique. “Secondary key” can have other meanings elsewhere; this course uses Hodder’s definition.

details.title: Names can repeat. Student IDs cannot.
Primary key: one reliable identifier
details.text: StudentID uniquely identifies a student. Even if two students have the same name, StudentID must not repeat. We choose it as the primary key (PK). A candidate key is any minimal attribute or combination that could uniquely identify a row. If SchoolEmail is also guaranteed unique, it could be another candidate key. In this Hodder chapter, an unchosen alternative is called a secondary key.
details.uz: Ikkita o‘quvchining ismi bir xil bo‘lishi mumkin. StudentID esa har birini alohida aniqlaydi.

details.title: Follow a foreign key
Foreign key and referential integrity
details.text: Student.ClassID is a foreign key (FK) because it refers to Class.ClassID (the primary key). Many students may use the same ClassID. Referential integrity means a non-null FK must match an existing parent key. In our example, 9Z is invalid because Class has only 7A and 7B.
details.uz: Foreign key boshqa jadvaldagi primary key bilan bog‘laydi. 9Z mavjud bo‘lmagani uchun mos yozuv topilmaydi.

details.title: Two remaining key ideas
rows: In StudentSubject, (StudentID, SubjectName) together uniquely identify one subject choice.
An index on ClassID and SecondName can speed up searching and sorting student lists. It does not replace the primary key.

details.title: The Elements example
details.text: Hodder’s small Elements table treats Symbol, Name and Atomic Weight as unique candidate keys, chooses Symbol as the primary key, and calls the others secondary keys. That is the example’s assumption. In a real design, validate uniqueness and stability rather than inferring them from a short sample.

worked.prompt: StudentSubject contains (S1276, Maths), (S1276, History) and (S1277, Maths). Why use a composite primary key?
worked.answer: StudentID repeats and SubjectName repeats, so neither alone identifies a choice. The pair uniquely identifies each student–subject choice, assuming a student takes each subject once.
criteria: The pair is unique under the rule.

checks.prompt: A new Student row has ClassID 9Z, but Class contains only 7A and 7B. What goes wrong?
checks.why: A non-null foreign key must match an existing referenced key.

checks.prompt: A student chooses both Maths and History. Why can (StudentID, SubjectName) be a composite key in StudentSubject?
checks.answer: The same StudentID can appear in several choices, and the same SubjectName can belong to several students. The pair identifies one student–subject choice uniquely.
criteria: Explain why StudentID alone is not enough.
Explain why the combination identifies the row.

lessons.title: One-to-many, step by step
lessons.subtitle: Count both directions before drawing a relationship.
objectives: Read 1:1, 1:m, m:1 and m:m relationships.
Distinguish optional from mandatory participation.
Resolve a many-to-many relationship with a linking table.
lessons.hook: One class has many students. Does that mean one student has many classes in this tutor-group model?

blocks.title: Count the link in both directions
blocks.text: A relationship describes how entities are connected. Here one Class has many Students: a one-to-many relationship. Read the same link backwards: many Students belong to one Class.
blocks.uz: Bitta sinfda nechta o‘quvchi? Ko‘p. Bitta o‘quvchi nechta asosiy sinfga tegishli? Bu misolda bitta. Demak Class dan Student ga — one-to-many. Yo‘nalishni almashtirsak — many-to-one.

blocks.title: An E-R diagram draws these rules
blocks.text: An entity-relationship (E-R) diagram represents entities and the links between them. Label the Class–Student link “one” at Class and “many” at Student. Cardinality tells us how many instances may participate. For example, one student has exactly one tutor class in this model.
blocks.uz: E-R diagram entity lar va ularning aloqasini chizib ko‘rsatadi. Class tomoniga 1, Student tomoniga many qo‘yiladi. Cardinality — bog‘lanishda nechta obyekt qatnashishi mumkinligi.

blocks.title: Can there be none?
rows: A desk may be empty or assigned to one employee.
A student must have one tutor class.
A new class can initially have no students.
An active team must have at least one player.
blocks.text: The first number is the minimum. Zero means optional; one means required. The second part is the maximum. Crow’s-foot diagrams use a circle for zero, a bar for one and a fork for many.
blocks.uz: Birinchi son — eng kam miqdor. 0 bo‘lsa qatnashmasligi ham mumkin, 1 bo‘lsa kamida bittasi shart. Oxirgi belgi — eng ko‘p miqdor. Crow’s-foot chizmada doira 0, chiziq 1, uch shox esa many ni bildiradi.

blocks.title: Students and subjects work differently
blocks.text: Noor has several subjects. Maths has several students. That is many-to-many. Store each pair in StudentSubject. Now Student → StudentSubject is one-to-many, and Subject → StudentSubject is one-to-many.
blocks.uz: Bitta o‘quvchi ko‘p fan oladi; bitta fanni ko‘p o‘quvchi oladi. O‘rtada StudentSubject jadvali har bir juftlikni saqlaydi. Natijada ikkita one-to-many aloqa hosil bo‘ladi.

blocks.title: Add the teacher using the same idea
blocks.text: Give each teacher a unique LicenceNumber. Store that value in Class to say who teaches the class. In this model, each class has one tutor; a teacher may have zero or several classes. Teacher.LicenceNumber is the primary key, and Class.LicenceNumber is a foreign key.
blocks.uz: O‘qituvchi uchun LicenceNumber yagona raqam bo‘lsin. Sinfga qaysi o‘qituvchi biriktirilganini Class ichidagi shu raqam orqali yozamiz. Yangi o‘qituvchida hali sinf bo‘lmasligi mumkin: uning sinflari 0..many.

worked.prompt: Noor and Ahmad take Maths; Noor also takes History. Why do we need StudentSubject?
worked.answer: One student has several subjects and one subject has several students. StudentSubject stores the three pairs separately, linking each student to each choice.

checks.prompt: Which structure implements Student ↔ Subject many-to-many membership?
options: Put all subject names in one Student cell
checks.why: The linking table stores one pair per row and preserves both one-to-many links.

checks.prompt: A new class can have no students yet. What is its student count range?
checks.why: Zero is permitted, and later the class can have several students.

recap: Relationship direction matters.
Minimum participation tells you whether a link is optional.
A linking table resolves many-to-many membership.
lessons.mistake: Do not infer minimum participation from “many” alone. A newly created class may allow zero students.

details.title: First, say the relationship in words
One-to-many is not a difficult formula
details.text: One Class can have many Students. In this model, each Student belongs to one Class. We draw two entities, Class and Student, with a line showing that relationship. An E-R diagram is simply a picture of entities and how they relate.
details.uz: Bir Class ichida bir nechta Student bo‘lishi mumkin; har bir Student bitta Classga tegishli.

details.title: Cardinality: how many can be connected?
rows: A new Class may have no Students yet
Each Student must belong to one Class in this model

details.title: Make the school diagram in three small moves

items.title: Draw Class → Student
items.text: Class has ClassID (PK). Student stores ClassID (FK). Label the relationship one-to-many.

items.title: Add Teacher
items.text: Teacher has LicenceNumber (PK). Class stores LicenceNumber (FK). One Teacher may teach several Classes.

items.title: Connect subjects
items.text: A Student may study several Subjects. Put one row per choice into StudentSubject to resolve the many-to-many relationship.

details.title: Optional and mandatory must follow the scenario
details.text: Mandatory means a related record is required; optional means it may be absent. These are assumptions of the school model, not universal rules for every school database. Hodder Figure 8.3 shows the initial Class–Student relationship; Activity 8B adds Teacher.

details.title: Explore the wider school model
details.text: Start with the class–student link, then open the five-table diagram when you are ready.

worked.prompt: Draw the teacher–class relationship and explain optionality for a newly recruited teacher with no class yet.
worked.answer: TEACHER(LicenceNumber PK) → CLASS(ClassID PK, LicenceNumber FK). Each class has exactly one tutor; a teacher may have zero or many classes. The class end is 0..many when read from one teacher.
criteria: Zero classes permitted for the teacher.

checks.prompt: One class has 26 students. One student belongs to one class. Which relationship describes Class → Student?
checks.why: A single Class row can be referenced by many Student rows.

checks.prompt: A student can study several subjects, and each subject can have many students. Which extra table should be created and why?
checks.answer: Create StudentSubject with StudentID and SubjectName to store each student–subject pairing, resolving a many-to-many relationship.
criteria: Name the StudentSubject linking table and its purpose.

lessons.title: 1NF: remove the subject list
lessons.subtitle: Move one repeating group, keeping the student link.
objectives: Identify repeating groups and update/deletion problems.
Convert the school example to 1NF.
Choose keys for the resulting tables.
lessons.hook: Noor studies Maths, History and Geography. Should all three be stored in one SubjectName cell?

blocks.title: Noor takes two subjects. Where should they go?
blocks.text: The Subjects cell contains a list. Finding every Maths student or adding another subject becomes awkward. Adding Subject1, Subject2 and Subject3 columns creates another repeating group.
blocks.uz: Noorning Subjects katagida ikkita fan bor. Bu ro‘yxatdan Maths olganlarni topish yoki yangi fan qo‘shish noqulay. Subject1, Subject2 kabi ustunlar ham takrorlanuvchi guruh hosil qiladi.

blocks.title: Normalisation gives the facts a better home
blocks.text: Normalisation organises tables to reduce unnecessary repetition and the problems it causes. We do it in stages. First normal form (1NF) requires single values and no repeating groups. Start by separating the repeated subject choices.
blocks.uz: Normalisation — jadvallarni ortiqcha takrorlash va undan keladigan muammolarni kamaytiradigan qilib tartiblash. Birinchi qadam 1NF: har katakda bitta qiymat, takrorlanuvchi guruhlar yo‘q. Hozir faqat shu qadamni bajaramiz.

blocks.title: Keep each student once in Student
blocks.text: Keep the student’s own facts here. StudentID remains the primary key. Noor’s name does not need a new copy whenever Noor adds a subject.
blocks.uz: O‘quvchining o‘ziga tegishli ma’lumotlari Student da qoladi. Fan qo‘shilgani uchun Noorning ismini yana bir qatorga ko‘chirmaymiz.

blocks.title: Put each subject choice on its own row
blocks.text: This StudentSubject table has one subject per row. StudentID preserves which student made the choice. The pair (StudentID, SubjectName) is its key. Both tables now have single values and no repeating groups.
blocks.uz: Har bir fan tanlovi alohida qatorga chiqdi. StudentID kim tanlaganini yo‘qotmaslik uchun saqlandi. Qatorni StudentID va SubjectName birga aniqlaydi. Hozircha Mr Yee takrorlanmoqda — bu keyingi bosqichda tuzatiladi.

blocks.title: Add one subject by adding one row
blocks.text: If Noor takes Science, add (S1276, Science, Miss Yo) to StudentSubject. Do not add a Subject3 column. 1NF fixes the repeating group; it does not yet remove every repeated fact.
blocks.uz: Noor Science olsa, StudentSubject ga bitta yangi qator qo‘shamiz. Yangi ustun ochmaymiz. 1NF ga o‘tish barcha ortiqcha takrorlanish tugadi degani emas.
blocks.remember: 1NF: one value per cell; no repeating groups.

worked.prompt: Noor adds Science after the table is in 1NF. What changes?
worked.answer: Add one StudentSubject row: (S1276, Science, Miss Yo). Keep Noor’s existing Student row. Do not add a Subject3 column.

checks.prompt: Which design still breaks 1NF?
options: Subject1, Subject2, Subject3 columns for an arbitrary list of choices
StudentID repeating in the child table
checks.why: A fixed series of subject columns is a repeating group; repeating an FK across separate rows is allowed.

checks.prompt: Noor adds a fourth subject. In the 1NF design, what do you add?
options: A new StudentSubject row linked to S1276
A second copy of Noor’s whole Student row
checks.why: Each subject choice is its own row. StudentID preserves who made the choice.

recap: 1NF: one value per cell; no repeating groups.
lessons.mistake: 1NF does not mean every value is unique. It means no repeating groups and atomic attribute values.
lessons.next: Next: 2NF and 3NF: where does each fact belong?.

details.title: Before: a repeating group (UNF)
Why this causes trouble
details.text: The first row contains a list of subjects and a parallel list of teachers. Searching for one subject or changing one teacher is awkward. Normalisation means reorganising data into suitable tables so unnecessary repetition and problematic dependencies are reduced.
details.uz: Bitta katakda bir nechta subject saqlash o‘rniga har bir tanlovni alohida qatorda yozamiz.

details.title: After: one student–subject choice per row
How to reach First normal form (1NF)

items.title: Find a repeated group
items.text: SubjectName contains the list 'Maths, History'.

items.title: Separate the choices
items.text: Create one row for each StudentID and SubjectName pair.

items.title: Keep the link
items.text: Retain StudentID in every subject-choice row so we know who chose each subject.

items.title: Check the key
items.text: (StudentID, SubjectName) identifies one row when a student cannot select the same subject twice.

details.title: What 1NF has NOT solved yet
details.text: The teacher for Maths still appears on multiple rows. 1NF removes repeating groups, but other dependencies remain. They are addressed by 2NF and 3NF in the next lesson.

details.title: Relations after the first step
details.text:
STUDENT(StudentID PK, FirstName, SecondName, DateOfBirth,
        ClassID, Location, TeacherName, LicenceNumber,
        Address, TeacherDateOfBirth)
STUDENTSUBJECT(StudentID PK/FK, SubjectName PK, SubjectTeacher)
details.note: PK/FK labels are design notation, not executable SQL.

worked.prompt: Noor adds Science. What is stored, and what stays unchanged?
worked.answer: Add (S1276, Science, Miss Yo) to StudentSubject. Do not add a new Subject4 column or a second full Student record. The StudentSubject key is (StudentID, SubjectName).

checks.prompt: Which SubjectName entry violates the no-repeating-groups rule?
checks.why: One cell contains several separate subject choices.

checks.prompt: Why is StudentID alone not a suitable primary key for the StudentSubject table?
checks.answer: A student can choose several subjects, so StudentID must repeat. The pair (StudentID, SubjectName) identifies each choice uniquely.

lessons.title: 2NF and 3NF: where does each fact belong?
lessons.subtitle: Separate subject facts, then class and teacher facts.
objectives: Remove a partial dependency to reach 2NF.
Remove non-key dependencies to reach 3NF.
Transfer the method to a new scenario.
lessons.hook: Does the Maths teacher depend on which student takes Maths?

blocks.title: Start with the 1NF table you just made
blocks.text: The key is (StudentID, SubjectName). Assume each subject has one teacher. Knowing Maths is enough to know Mr Yee; the student’s ID is not needed. SubjectTeacher depends on only part of the key. This is a partial dependency.
blocks.uz: Kalit ikki qismli: StudentID + SubjectName. Lekin Maths o‘qituvchisini topish uchun StudentID kerak emas. Faqat SubjectName yetadi. Demak o‘qituvchi butun kalitga emas, bir qismiga bog‘liq.

blocks.title: 2NF: move the fact that depends on only SubjectName
blocks.text: Create Subject with one teacher per subject. Remove SubjectTeacher from StudentSubject; keep the student–subject pairs there. Second normal form means 1NF with no non-key attribute depending on just part of a candidate key.
blocks.uz: Subject jadvalida har fan o‘qituvchisini bir marta saqlaymiz. StudentSubject da esa faqat o‘quvchi–fan juftligi qoladi. 2NF uchun 1NF bo‘lishi va non-key attribute kalitning bir qismiga qaram bo‘lmasligi kerak.
blocks.remember: 2NF: a non-key fact must not depend on only part of a key.

blocks.title: A different problem: the classroom follows the class
blocks.text: StudentID tells us the class; ClassID tells us the room. Location therefore depends on ClassID, another non-key attribute in this table. This indirect link is a transitive dependency.
blocks.uz: StudentID orqali sinfni bilamiz. Sinf orqali xonani bilamiz. Location o‘quvchining o‘ziga emas, ClassID ga tegishli. Bu kalitdan boshqa ustun orqali keladigan bog‘liqlik — transitive dependency.

blocks.title: 3NF: store the room with the class
blocks.text: Move Location into Class. Student keeps StudentID and ClassID, so the link survives. Third normal form means 2NF with no transitive dependency of a non-key attribute on a key.
blocks.uz: Location ni Class ga ko‘chiramiz. Student da ClassID qolishi shart — aks holda o‘quvchining sinfini yo‘qotamiz. 3NF — 2NF bo‘lishi va non-key attribute ning kalitga boshqa non-key attribute orqali bog‘lanmasligi.
blocks.remember: 3NF: put class facts with Class, and student facts with Student.

blocks.title: Apply the same question to teacher details
blocks.text: A teacher’s address and birth date depend on LicenceNumber. Store them once in Teacher. Class keeps LicenceNumber to identify its tutor; Subject keeps LicenceNumber to identify its teacher. This gives five tables: Student, Class, Teacher, Subject and StudentSubject.
blocks.uz: O‘qituvchining manzili va tug‘ilgan sanasi LicenceNumber ga bog‘liq. Ular Teacher da saqlanadi. Class va Subject ichida shu o‘qituvchiga bog‘laydigan LicenceNumber qoladi. Endi to‘liq beshta jadval sxemasini ko‘rish mumkin.

worked.prompt: Student contains StudentID, ClassID and Location. Why move Location to Class?
worked.answer: The room is a fact about the class. Several students in 7A repeat Room 12. Store (7A, Room 12) once in Class and keep ClassID in Student so the relationship survives.

checks.prompt: Which dependency prevents StudentSubject(StudentID, SubjectName, SubjectTeacher) from being in 2NF?
checks.why: The non-key teacher depends on only part of the composite key.

checks.prompt: After Location moves to Class, what must Student keep?
checks.why: ClassID preserves the link from each student to the correct class.

recap: 2NF: a non-key fact must not depend on only part of a key.
3NF: put class facts with Class, and student facts with Student.
lessons.mistake: Do not split tables without identifying a dependency. Normalisation follows the business rules, not just the appearance of the data.

details.title: Start with the 1NF subject choices
2NF: the fact must depend on the whole key
details.text: The key here is (StudentID, SubjectName). Under the book's example, SubjectTeacher depends on SubjectName only, not on which student chose it. This is a partial dependency. Put SubjectName and SubjectTeacher into a separate Subject table. Keep only StudentID and SubjectName in StudentSubject.
details.uz: Maths o‘qituvchisi StudentIDga emas, SubjectNamega bog‘liq. Shuning uchun SubjectTeacher alohida Subject jadvaliga o‘tadi.

details.title: After 2NF: split the repeated teacher fact
3NF: remove dependencies between non-key facts
details.text: In the wide Student table, StudentID determines ClassID, while ClassID determines Location. Location belongs to Class, not directly to Student. Similarly, a teacher's address belongs to Teacher, identified by LicenceNumber. Splitting these facts into their own tables removes non-key dependencies.
details.uz: Classning xonasi Studentning o‘ziga emas, ClassIDga bog‘liq. Locationni Class jadvaliga ajratamiz.

details.title: Final design — one job for each table
One test for each normal form

items.title: 1NF
items.text: Do any fields contain repeating groups? If yes, separate them.

items.title: 2NF
items.text: For a composite key, does a non-key fact depend on only part of it? If yes, move that fact.

items.title: 3NF
items.text: Does a non-key fact depend on another non-key fact? If yes, move it to the appropriate table.

details.title: Final school relations — PK/FK design notation
details.text:
STUDENT(StudentID PK, FirstName, SecondName, DateOfBirth, ClassID FK)
CLASS(ClassID PK, Location, LicenceNumber FK)
TEACHER(LicenceNumber PK, TeacherName, Address, TeacherDateOfBirth)
STUDENTSUBJECT(StudentID PK/FK, SubjectName PK/FK)
SUBJECT(SubjectName PK, LicenceNumber FK)
details.note: ClassID is retained in STUDENT so the student–class relationship survives. The abbreviated list on Hodder p.207 omits it.

details.title: The model depends on the rules — Extension 8B
details.text: If the same subject can have several teachers or levels, SubjectName → LicenceNumber is no longer a valid dependency. Introduce CourseOffering(OfferingID, SubjectName, Level, LicenceNumber) and link enrolments to OfferingID. This is an extension of the simplified source model.

details.title: Transfer to employees and contacts — Activity 8D
details.text: An employee can have several contacts, and one contact can belong to several employees. Store EMPLOYEE(EmployeeNumber PK, EmployeeName, Position), CONTACT(ContactNumber PK, ContactName, ContactEmailAddress), and EMPLOYEECONTACT(EmployeeNumber PK/FK, ContactNumber PK/FK). The linking table resolves the many-to-many relationship.

worked.prompt: Activity 8E adaptation: each warehouse part has one manufacturer. Design relations for PartNumber, Description, DateLastOrdered, MinimumOrderLevel, ManufacturerName, ManufacturerAddress, ManufacturerContact, WarehousePosition and StockCount.
worked.answer: PART(PartNumber PK, Description, DateLastOrdered, MinimumOrderLevel, ManufacturerID FK, WarehousePosition, StockCount); MANUFACTURER(ManufacturerID PK, ManufacturerName, ManufacturerAddress, ManufacturerContact). One manufacturer supplies many parts. ManufacturerID is an added stable identifier; using a guaranteed-unique ManufacturerName is another defensible stated assumption.

checks.prompt: SubjectTeacher depends only on SubjectName, which is part of (StudentID, SubjectName). What must be removed to reach 2NF?
checks.why: The teacher fact depends on only part of the composite key.

checks.prompt: A teacher changes their address. Which table should be updated in the final 3NF design, and why?
checks.answer: Update Teacher once using LicenceNumber. Address depends on the teacher, not on any individual student, class or subject choice.
criteria: Explain why one update is sufficient.

lessons.title: Database or DBMS?
lessons.subtitle: Data, software, rules and the design.
objectives: Distinguish a database from a DBMS.
Identify metadata held in a data dictionary.
Explain data modelling and a logical schema.
lessons.hook: “StudentID is a VARCHAR(5) primary key.” Is that a student’s data, or data about the database?

blocks.title: The stored names are not the software
blocks.text: Noor, Ahmad and their classes are data in a database. The software that stores, retrieves and changes those records is a database management system (DBMS). Data management means organising and maintaining data so it can provide useful information.
blocks.uz: O‘quvchilar haqidagi ma’lumotlar — database ichida. Ularni saqlaydigan, topadigan va o‘zgartiradigan dastur — DBMS. Ma’lumotni tartibli saqlash va yangilab borish data management deyiladi.
blocks.remember: Database = organised data. DBMS = software that manages it.

blocks.title: A value is different from a rule about that value
blocks.text: Descriptions of data are metadata. A data dictionary stores metadata such as table and field names, types, sizes, validation rules, keys, relationships, indexes and storage information.
blocks.uz: Noor — ma’lumotning o‘zi. “FirstName matn saqlaydi” — ma’lumot haqidagi tavsif. Bunday tavsiflar metadata deyiladi; data dictionary ularning nomi, turi, cheklovi, kaliti va bog‘lanishlarini saqlaydi.

blocks.title: The DBMS checks the recorded rules
blocks.text: If StudentID must be unique, the DBMS can reject a second S1276. If ClassID must reference Class, it can reject 9Z. These checks protect integrity. They cannot tell whether a plausible but incorrectly typed birth date is the person’s real birthday.
blocks.uz: DBMS qoidaga qarab takrorlangan StudentID yoki mavjud bo‘lmagan 9Z sinfini rad qiladi. Lekin ko‘rinishidan to‘g‘ri kiritilgan sana haqiqiy tug‘ilgan kun ekanini o‘zi bilmaydi.

blocks.title: Plan the facts before creating the tables
blocks.text: Deciding which entities, attributes and relationships the school needs is data modelling. The logical schema is the resulting design: tables, their attributes, keys and constraints. It describes the design without choosing a particular DBMS.
blocks.uz: Qaysi obyekt, xususiyat va aloqa kerakligini aniqlash — data modelling. Shu rejaning jadvallar, ustunlar, kalitlar va qoidalar ko‘rinishidagi tavsifi — logical schema. U hali aniq DBMS tanlashga bog‘liq emas.

worked.prompt: Is “Noor” the same kind of information as “StudentID must be unique”?
worked.answer: Noor is stored data. “StudentID must be unique” describes a rule: metadata. The data dictionary stores that rule, and the DBMS can enforce it.

checks.prompt: Which belongs in a data dictionary?
options: The type and validation rule for ExamMark
checks.why: The dictionary describes the structure and rules, not the actual exam results.

checks.prompt: Which is the DBMS?
options: The software that manages records and enforces rules
checks.why: The database contains the data. The DBMS is the software that manages it.

recap: Database = organised data. DBMS = software that manages it.
lessons.mistake: Do not describe a data dictionary as a list of student records. It describes those records’ structure.
lessons.next: Next: Who may see or change the data?.

details.title: The Student data the school already understands
Database and DBMS are not the same thing
details.text: A database stores organised data, such as the Student rows above. A database management system (DBMS) is the system software that lets authorised applications create, read, change and manage that data. Data management means keeping that data organised and maintained so useful information can be produced.
details.uz: Database — ma'lumotlarning o'zi. DBMS — shu ma'lumotni boshqaradigan dastur. Ular bir narsa emas.

details.title: Follow one ordinary school change

items.title: A new class is recorded
items.text: The school creates Class 7C. The DBMS stores the record according to the defined table rules.

items.title: Noor moves from 7A to 7C
items.text: An authorised user changes Noor's ClassID in the shared Student table.

items.title: Everyone sees the controlled value
items.text: Attendance and Exams can read the same updated class, rather than separate copies.

details.title: Data dictionary: descriptions, not student records
rows: ClassID is a foreign key to Class
DateOfBirth is defined as a date
Rules, relationships, indexes and storage details

details.title: Data modelling and logical schema
details.text: Before building the database, the designer decides which entities and attributes are needed and how they relate. This is data modelling; an E-R diagram is one way to show the model. A logical schema might say STUDENT(StudentID PK, FirstName, ClassID FK) and CLASS(ClassID PK, Location). It describes the database design independently of whether the school uses MySQL, SQLite or another DBMS.
details.uz: Data modelling — jadval va bog'lanishlarni oldindan rejalash. Logical schema — qaysi jadvallar va kalitlar kerakligini ifodalovchi reja.

details.title: Why a DBMS is better than separate files
details.text: Linked tables reduce unnecessary duplicated facts (data redundancy). One controlled update reduces disagreements (data inconsistency). DBMS-managed structures and queries reduce dependence on a particular application's file layout (data dependency). Foreign-key values may legitimately repeat because they provide the links.
details.uz: Yodlashdan oldin sababini ko'ring: bitta to'g'ri yangilanish barcha ruxsatli dasturlarga ko'rinadi.

worked.prompt: Classify these items: Noor; StudentID is a primary key; an E-R diagram of Student and Class.
worked.answer: Noor is stored application data. The primary-key declaration is metadata in the data dictionary. The E-R diagram is a data model; with detailed relations and constraints it contributes to the logical schema.

checks.prompt: Which item belongs in a data dictionary rather than a Student record?
checks.why: The dictionary stores definitions and rules. Actual student values belong in tables.

checks.prompt: Attendance and Exams once stored separate copies of every student's class. Explain one improvement provided by a shared DBMS.
checks.answer: The DBMS allows authorised applications to access the same Student record. Updating ClassID once reduces duplicated data and the risk of inconsistent class values across applications.
criteria: Explain one shared record or controlled update.
Link it to redundancy or inconsistency.

lessons.title: Who may see or change the data?
lessons.subtitle: Permissions first; then follow a database request.
objectives: Select security measures for a concrete risk.
Distinguish developer interface from query processor.
Trace DDL and DML through the query processor.
lessons.hook: A pupil needs their timetable. Should their account be able to delete the Student table?

blocks.title: Different people need different permissions
blocks.text: Access rights say what a user may read or change. A correct password identifies the account; it does not mean the account may do everything.
blocks.uz: Access rights foydalanuvchi nimani ko‘rishi va o‘zgartirishini belgilaydi. Parol kim kirganini tekshiradi. To‘g‘ri parol hamma narsani o‘chirishga ruxsat degani emas.

blocks.title: Match each protection to a problem
rows: Data needs the correct key to be readable.
We need to trace a change
Record who changed what and when.
blocks.text: These measures do different jobs. A backup helps recovery; it does not decide who may view the live database.
blocks.uz: Har himoya turi boshqa vazifani bajaradi. Backup yo‘qolgan ma’lumotni qaytaradi; kim ko‘rishi mumkinligini access rights belgilaydi. Audit log esa kim nima qilganini qayd etadi.

blocks.title: Where do database requests come from?
blocks.text: SQL means Structured Query Language. It is a language for database commands. A developer interface is where a developer enters those commands. A query processor is the DBMS component that handles them. A query-by-example form lets a user describe a request without writing SQL.
blocks.uz: SQL — bazaga buyruq berish tili. Developer interface — dasturchi buyruq yozadigan vosita. Query processor — shu buyruqni qayta ishlaydigan DBMS qismi. Oddiy foydalanuvchi esa ayrim so‘rovlarni SQL yozmasdan forma orqali berishi mumkin.

blocks.title: Follow one request through the processor
rows: Read the definition and record metadata.
Translate the request and optimise its execution.
blocks.text: DDL describes structure. DML retrieves or changes stored data. These are two kinds of SQL command. The next lesson compares them with small examples.
blocks.uz: DDL jadval tuzilishini belgilaydi. DML esa ichidagi ma’lumotni oladi yoki o‘zgartiradi. Query processor da tuzilma ta’rifi interpreter orqali, ma’lumot so‘rovi compiler va execution engine orqali ishlanadi.

worked.prompt: An administrator accidentally deletes valid data. Which protection helps restore it?
worked.answer: A usable backup provides a recovery copy. Access rights restrict who can make changes, but cannot by themselves recreate lost data.

checks.prompt: Which control helps restore data after loss?
checks.why: A backup is a recovery copy. Permissions and indexes serve different jobs.

checks.prompt: Trace a SELECT query from the developer’s interface to its result.
checks.answer: The interface accepts SQL; the DML compiler translates and optimises it; the query evaluation engine executes the instructions and produces the result.

recap: Access rights restrict actions and data visibility.
Backups, encryption and audit logs serve different purposes.
DDL records definitions; DML is compiled, optimised and evaluated.
lessons.mistake: A query processor is not the same thing as the screen where a developer types SQL.
lessons.next: Next: SQL: structure or stored data?.

details.title: Three users, three sensible permissions
rows: Use access beyond their assigned role

details.title: Logging in is only the first check
details.text: A username and password help identify or authenticate the user. Access rights then decide which tables, rows or views they can see and whether they may read, append, modify or delete data. A successful login does not give unrestricted access.
details.uz: Login: kim kirganini bilish. Access rights: qaysi ma'lumotni ko'rishi yoki o'zgartirishi mumkinligi.

details.title: Every security tool has a different job
